claims.text: Overall wear resistance of the FeNiCrCoCu coating at high temperature is governed by formation of a stable, coherent surface oxide layer.
Microscopic deformation of the FeNiCrCoCu coating during high-temperature sliding is governed by formation of a stable, coherent surface oxide layer.
The coherent oxide layer acts as a protective barrier against wear.
The coherent oxide layer acts as a protective barrier against microscopic deformation.
The baseline coating is 10 μm thick and has a surface roughness of 0.1 μm.
The controlled intervention increases coating thickness from 10 μm to 15 μm, a 50% increase.
The prediction is intended to hold at 500–700°C, a sliding speed of 1 m/s, and a normal load of 10 N.
The oxide forms through thermally activated diffusion and reaction of metal ions with oxygen.
Increasing coating thickness from 10 μm to 15 μm will increase wear resistance by 25% relative to the baseline.
Increasing coating thickness will decrease the wear rate from 10^-4 mm^3/Nm to 7.5^-4 mm^3/Nm.
Increasing coating thickness will reduce microscopic deformation by 30% relative to the baseline.
Increasing coating thickness will decrease deformation depth from 5 μm to 3.5 μm.
Wear and deformation may depend on the coating deposition method, substrate material, and testing conditions.
Oxide-layer formation may be influenced by humidity, atmospheric pressure, surface contamination, or all three.
A wear-rate increase of more than 10% after increasing coating thickness is designated as a falsifying result.
A deformation-depth increase of more than 15% after increasing coating thickness is designated as a falsifying result.

contradictions.description: The stated decrease from 10^-4 to 7.5^-4 mm^3/Nm is numerically inconsistent with a 25% reduction in wear rate. If 7.5^-4 means 7.5×10^-4, it is an increase; a 25% reduction from 1×10^-4 would be 7.5×10^-5 mm^3/Nm.
The notation 1.1^-4 mm^3/Nm is inconsistent with the stated 10% increase from 10^-4 mm^3/Nm. The intended value would be 1.1×10^-4 mm^3/Nm.
